prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state

statement.case_for: I keep B050 as my preferred prize and my configuration is unchanged from round 1 in its ballot and names. What has changed is how I would word the citation. Having read the full exchange, I would anchor it on the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall state, because that is where the credited names are exactly right: Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 classification and the time-reversal-protected helical edge states, and Molenkamp's HgTe/CdTe wells gave the quantised edge conductance that tested the prediction. Danielsson, Eriksson and Pearce word the experimental half as the first observation in HgTe wells, and I now prefer that over my own more generic round-1 wording, since it limits the claim to what the experiment showed and does not stretch it to three-dimensional materials. From the experimental side the maturity is not in doubt. Edge and surface states of this kind have been reproduced by independent transport, nonlocal and ARPES measurements in several material families over close to two decades, and microscopy and spectroscopy of the heterostructures have made the interface quality behind the HgTe result a matter of record. The prize criterion as I understand it is a discovery or invention with identifiable originators, and this is a case where a sharp prediction was followed by a measurable result.
statement.case_against: The weaknesses are real and round 1 did not remove them. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe quantum-well route that Molenkamp realised, and I cannot give the chair a fully satisfying answer to why they are outside the credited names. The best I can say is that the shortlisted achievement is the prediction of the time-reversal-invariant state and its first observation, and that the HgTe proposal refined where to look rather than what to look for. A critic can fairly reject that, and a three-name limit forces a cut that a historian of the field would not make. The experimental half also rests on a single material and group, with independent confirmation coming later and in other systems. The overlap with the 2016 prize for topological phases and phase transitions remains an argument the committee must be willing to make explicitly, not assume. Finally, I should not mistake the size of the B050 group for evidence: four of us moved to it after reading each other's opening ballots, and the chair is right that this is a stated preference rather than accumulated support.

responses.point: Kroll argues that B050 opened a new organising principle whereas the clock opened a new level of accuracy, and that the committee has to say which criterion ranks higher; his own preference stays with the optical lattice clock because of its clean two-name credit.
responses.response: I accept the framing and I would not call B051 weak science. The magic-wavelength argument is a genuinely different idea from the single-ion work of 2012, and I am persuaded on that point more than I was in round 1. But I think the criterion cuts toward B050. A prize rewards a discovery or invention, and B050 contains both a conceptual novelty and a measured quantity with no earlier prize behind it, while for the clock the committee would have to argue priority over 2005 and 2012 and wait on a redefinition of the second that you rightly say should not decide the matter. I would take a defensible attribution problem over a defensible novelty problem, because the first can be handled by a narrow citation and the second goes to the heart of what the prize is for. If the committee judged the BHZ omission to be disqualifying, I would move to B051 before any other option, which is why it is my first alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth holds B051 first for conceptual clarity and the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and answers my round-1 priority concern by saying that the magic-wavelength lattice is a new principle which made neutral-atom ensembles competitive with single ions.
responses.response: Your answer to the priority concern is fair and I have weighed it. I do not think the clock is a refinement in the dismissive sense, and I take your point that no candidate here has a perfectly exhaustive credit, including my own earlier first choice. Where we still differ is on what the citation can safely say. For the clock the claim to be written narrowly is a claim about precision, and the committee would be defending a metrological advance whose practical consequence, the redefinition of the second, is still prospective. For B050 the observable and its independent confirmations already exist in the laboratory. I also want to answer your question to me directly: my round-1 ranking of B051 low reflected a view on novelty relative to earlier prizes, not distance from the field or doubt about the measurements, and that view has softened but not reversed.

responses.point: Eriksson wants the citation to say explicitly that Kane and Mele supplied a time-reversal-invariant state with no net magnetic field, which the 2016 work did not anticipate, so that the committee can defend the distinction from the earlier prize, and he keeps Molenkamp in the configuration.
responses.response: I agree and would write that distinction into the citation rather than leave it to the committee's explanatory text. The quantum spin Hall state is a topological state that exists without a magnetic field and is protected by time-reversal symmetry, a different symmetry class from the integer quantum Hall topology that 2016 recognised. I also agree with you on keeping the experiment. Where I would add caution is on your fallback logic: you name B002 or B051 if the attribution fails, and I share B002 as a second alternative, but I would not describe the omission of the BHZ proposal as making B050 wrong. It makes it imperfect, and every serious candidate on this list is imperfect in credit.

responses.point: Danielsson supports B050 as a prediction that nature confirmed, and offers a theory-only Kane-Mele prize as the fallback if the attribution proves indefensible, while asking whether the 2D effect or 3D materials should anchor the citation.
responses.response: I would not accept the theory-only fallback. The Kane-Mele prediction was one of several competing proposals for a spin Hall state until the HgTe wells gave quantised edge conductance, and a prize without the measurement would drop the part that made it a discovery. On your anchoring question, I now think the 2D quantum spin Hall effect is the right anchor, and I would keep the three-dimensional insulators out of the citation. The credited names do not include Fu, Moore, Balents or Hasan, and a citation that claimed the 3D materials would invite exactly the omission argument we are trying to avoid. A narrow 2D citation is smaller than the full history, but it is accurate to the three named people.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B050 from his own B009 and warns that B050 is the safe consensus choice, so the committee should not mistake safety for being the best science on the list; he names B051 as his fallback.
responses.response: I take the warning seriously and it is the same one I made to myself about my own move from the quantum cascade laser. My response is that the support for B050 comes from different directions, theory, atomic physics and experiment, and four of us gave scientific reasons, not only counting. That does not make it the best science on the list, and I would not claim that. It makes it the discovery I can defend most readily against the prize criterion, which is a narrower test and the one I think the committee is applying.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can defend omitting Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal preceded and enabled the Molenkamp experiment, and whether that omission damages the experimental half of the citation.

Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases is judged sufficiently distinct from the quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 classification, which I believe is true but cannot demonstrate to a sceptical colleague.

Whether the 2D quantum spin Hall effect is the right anchor given that three-dimensional topological insulators arguably had the larger materials impact, and whether a narrow citation looks too small for a prize.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be allowed to delay B051; I do not think it should, but I have not reached a view that would put the clock ahead of B050.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the preferred configuration or the alternatives. I am a Chalmers colleague of Goran Johansson, who prefers B015 and keeps B038 only as an alternative and has said he is recused from B038; none of the credited names on B050, B051 or B002 is documented as being at Chalmers or as a close collaborator. I have documented ties to David R. Clarke (IBM) and to Japanese universities and the international microscopy federation, none of which touch the credited names. Hidetoshi Katori (B051) is Japan-based and I note this only as a general academic exchange connection, not a personal one. Nothing has changed since round 1.
